points.heading: Simple tenses
points.body: In the indicative mood, five simple tenses locate the action without a perfect auxiliary. The present names habits or what is happening now (I sing). The imperfect (or past progressive / used-to sense) paints background, habit, or ongoing past (I was singing / I used to sing). The preterite (simple past) marks a finished past event (I sang). The future places what has not yet happened (I will sing). The simple conditional expresses hypothesis, politeness, or a possible result (I would sing). Conjugate one regular verb through all five to see stem and endings clearly.

points.heading: Compound tenses
points.body: The five compound (perfect) tenses use an auxiliary + past participle. Present perfect (I have sung) links past action to present relevance. Pluperfect (I had sung) is a past before another past. Anterior preterite (I had sung — literary / rare) marks completion just before another past event. Future perfect (I will have sung) projects completion by a future point. Conditional perfect (I would have sung) marks what would have happened in a past hypothesis. The participle stays fixed; only the auxiliary changes.

points.heading: Usage: simple vs compound
points.body: Choose simple or compound by relative time and aspect. A closed past moment («Yesterday I finished») usually takes simple past. A result that still matters («I have already finished») takes present perfect. Imperfect/progressive paints the scene; simple past moves the plot. Pluperfect and conditional perfect place an action as «already done» relative to another anchor. Ask: finished point, background, or result still in force?

lesson.summary: Master the ten indicative tenses: five simple (present, imperfect, preterite, future, conditional) and five compound with auxiliary + participle, knowing when to choose each.
